# Mathematical reference

These pages define the mathematical models implemented by PhaseSmith's native
Rust kernels and exposed through both the Rust and Python APIs. Python does not
reimplement these production equations: its typed scripting interface calls the
same kernels used by native applications.

Equations use plain, copyable text so this reference works offline and does not
depend on JavaScript or an external math-rendering service.

## Coverage

| Area | Implemented mathematics |
| --- | --- |
| [Peak profiles](peak-profiles.md) | normalized pseudo-Voigt, TCH mixing, CW broadening, wavelength components, FCJ asymmetry, neutron TOF |
| [Crystallography](crystallography.md) | cell/reciprocal metrics, exact symmetry, reflection conditions, scattering factors, displacement factors, structure factors, LP corrections, Bragg positions |
| [Pattern composition](pattern-composition.md) | multi-phase and multi-wavelength sums, size, microstrain, preferred orientation, derivative products |
| [Backgrounds](backgrounds.md) | Smooth Bruckner preprocessing, polynomial, Chebyshev, point, amorphous, and composite backgrounds |
| [Refinement](refinement.md) | residuals, R factors, constraints, Le Bail redistribution, damped Gauss–Newton, covariance, and quantitative phase analysis |

Every section names the native Rust owner and corresponding public Python modules.
Models not
implemented by the current API—such as magnetic scattering, absorption,
extinction, and symmetry-refined anisotropic displacement—are not described as
available mathematics.

## Shared notation

- `x` is a sampled pattern coordinate.
- `φ = 2θ` is a diffraction angle; angular public APIs use degrees unless a
  formula explicitly says radians.
- `λ` and direct-cell lengths are in ångströms.
- `h = (h,k,l)^T` is a Miller-index column vector.
- `G` and `G* = G^-1` are direct and reciprocal metric tensors.
- `q² = h^T G* h = 1/d²`; `s = sqrt(q²)/2 = sin(θ)/λ`.
- `J v` and `J^T u` denote Jacobian-vector and transpose-Jacobian-vector
  products. They are analytical products, not finite differences.
